title: Still Operational
paragraphs: The first sound Andrew Walker heard that morning was singing.
It came from the kitchen at six fourteen, loud enough to carry down the corridor. Darius had a good voice when he wanted one. This morning he appeared to be inventing a song as he went.

From the other bed, Nicolas Vallée dragged a pillow over his face. Nico's oversized sleep shirt hung loosely from narrow shoulders, making him look even smaller than his five-foot-six frame. A riot of dark brown curls poked over the pillow.
“Does ’e know it's six in the morning?” Nico asked. His French accent was stronger when he was half asleep; the h in he hadn't made it out of bed either.
“He's making breakfast,” Andrew mumbled.
“He can make breakfast without giving us a concert. There must be a regulation against that.”
From the kitchen came another enthusiastic verse, followed by a loud metallic crash.
The singing stopped.
“Sorry!” Darius called from down the hall.
Nico lifted the edge of his pillow. “Non, non—was he apologizing to us or the pot? Because I think the pot got the better apology.”
“Knowing Darius? Both.”
“Good. The pot forgives him. I don't.”
Andrew laughed despite himself.
A moment later, Darius started singing again.
Nico stared at the ceiling. “Unbelievable.”

Nico lowered the pillow enough for Andrew to catch his hazel eyes, a scattering of freckles across his cheeks and small straight nose, and the familiar crooked grin. One side of his curls had been flattened against the mattress while the other stuck out wildly. Still grinning, he began tapping a rhythm against the metal bedframe with his fingertips.
“Now you're doing it,” Andrew said.
“Zat's different,” Nico said. “I'm keeping time. Entirely different thing.”
“For what?”
“The song I'm writing about the military's systematic denial of sleep.”
“Catchy title.”
“Working title. I'll shorten it for the album.”
Andrew reached for the clock above his pillow. It still read 06:14. He had been awake less than a minute and had already lost an argument he wasn't sure he'd joined.

Their sleeping room had once been a records office in a municipal maintenance depot. Two narrow bunks filled most of it; an old noticeboard had left a clean rectangle on the wall. A radiator made an occasional hopeful click without producing any heat. Andrew's uniform hung from a hook beside the door. On the shelf above his bed sat a torch, two secondhand novels, and a wristwatch he'd been meaning to repair.

Andrew swung his legs over the edge of the bunk. He was nineteen, lean and wiry rather than imposing, and his feet searched for the socks he'd left beside the bed. Running a military outpost was not among the things he'd imagined doing at his age.
His orders still listed him as acting commander.
Matthias Adler had led the unit when there were twelve of them. Andrew had been his second-in-command.
Now there were eight. His rank hadn't changed when Matthias died. Only his responsibilities had.
He pulled on his socks before his feet touched the cold floor. Across the room Nico had gone back to composing his song, this time without words.
Three knocks sounded at the door.
“Andrew?” Darius called. “Are you awake?”
“Not by choice,” Andrew answered.
“Could you taste something before breakfast?” Darius asked. The soft French rounding of his vowels was familiar, but his measured voice sounded nothing like Nico's restless chatter.
Nico pulled the pillow over his face again. “Whatever he wants you to try, tell him it's brilliant. Magnifique. Then he'll go away.”
Andrew opened the door.

Darius Okafor stood in the corridor wearing a flour-dusted apron stretched over his broad chest. At nineteen he was already six foot three, the tallest and broadest of the squad, with powerful shoulders that made the narrow doorway look poorly designed. He had deep brown skin, short, tightly curled black hair trimmed close at the sides, a broad nose, and gentle brown eyes set in a face that seemed perpetually on the verge of a shy smile. Flour coated his large hands, which were more often marked by garden soil or small cooking burns than by anything from the range. In one hand he carried a spoon; in the other, a little bowl of porridge that looked almost comically small against his fingers. Warm cinnamon drifted toward Andrew.
“I used the last of the apples,” Darius said. “Would you tell me if it's too sweet?”
Andrew accepted a spoonful. The porridge was thick and hot, with pieces of apple that still held their shape. He swallowed, then took a second taste before returning the spoon.
“Don't change anything,” Andrew said.
Darius's face eased into a smile. “Not even a little more cinnamon, hm?”
“If you have more cinnamon, hide it before Nico finds out.”
“I'm awake,” Nico called from the room. “And I can hear you insulting me.”
“Allez, get dressed,” Darius called back. “Breakfast at seven. I'll keep it warm.”

Andrew watched him hurry toward the kitchen, humming again. Darius was the unit's designated supply hand as well as its self-appointed cook, and he took both jobs seriously. Last week he'd bartered two loaves of bread for a driver's bruised apples; she'd wanted something fresh for her children, and the flour he'd given up wasn't easily replaced. He'd turned what might have been a snack into breakfast for eight.
Andrew shut the door.
Nico lowered his pillow once more. “All right, tell me. Was it actually good?”
“Unfortunately.”
“Why unfortunately?”
“Now we have to help with the dishes.”
Nico sat up. “Ah, zut. That's extortion. He feeds us, then we're expected to work for him?”
“Tell him that when you ask for seconds.”

In the washroom Andrew faced a spotted mirror and tried to flatten his thick, dark waves. Someone in the unit had cut them unevenly around his ears, and the result looked no better this morning. His warm olive-toned face, straight nose, defined jaw, and brown eyes under expressive dark brows looked younger than the stubble he kept forgetting to shave. He gave up, pulled on his uniform and stepped into the waking outpost. Pipes ticked in the walls. A radio was on in the common room. Through a rain-streaked window he could see the hangar across the courtyard, its doors framed by concrete barriers and cable runs. The mechs inside were among the reasons people could still live behind this part of the defensive perimeter.

The depot stood in Germany, inside the last territory humanity had managed to keep from the Reclaimed. Elsewhere the defenses had fallen; survivors had made their way here from countries that no longer had a safe place to offer them. The enemy was no rumor or mysterious name. Andrew had seen the human tissue joined to machinery, and the way a mass of those things could move together as if receiving one thought. He would be perfectly happy not to see them before breakfast.

The broadcast mentioned another eastern road closure, a civilian supply convoy held overnight after the relay went silent, and new restrictions on fuel and cooking oil. The announcer gave the hours when people could exchange ration slips for water. Nobody at the depot stopped to listen to these bulletins anymore, though everybody heard them.

On his way past the noticeboard, Andrew noticed a fresh handwritten offer pinned beneath the duty schedule: NEED WINTER BOOTS, SIZE 43. CAN REPAIR TWO HEATERS OR TRADE SOAP. There were three more notes beside it, each listing what someone needed and what they had to offer. Nobody had written a price.
In the common room, Akari Sato was taking a photograph of an empty chair.

Akari rose from her crouch and stepped sideways to adjust the camera before taking another picture. She was petite, barely five foot four, with a slender, athletic build and so much restless energy that standing still seemed to be an effort. Her long, straight black hair was pulled into a high ponytail, already slipping loose at the neck, with wisps framing an oval face and a small, delicate nose. Dark brown eyes followed every change in the light, and her bright smile suggested she'd already thought of something amusing. A faded sweatshirt hung off one shoulder, one sleeve pushed above the elbow; dark trousers and a worn camera strap completed an outfit she'd clearly assembled for comfort rather than inspection. Akari was the unit's reconnaissance specialist, which explained her eye for detail, if not her fascination with chairs.
Andrew stopped. “Should I ask what that chair did?”
“I'm testing the light,” Akari said quickly, the lilting rhythm of her English rising with her excitement. “See? Look how it catches the edge of the chair.”
“It seems to be behaving.”
“Unlike the rest of you. The chair actually holds still.”

A paperback lay on the nearby table. Sera Bell sat beside it, sorting Akari's photographs into two careful piles. Slender and a little under five foot six, she had medium-brown skin, a softly rounded nose, and full lips that pressed together whenever a picture failed her inspection. Long, dark curls were gathered into a loose bun, though a few escaped beside her cheeks. Amber-brown eyes, almost golden where the morning light caught them, moved from one photograph to the next with the same careful attention she gave the XR-17s' electronic diagnostics. An oversized dark sweater swallowed her narrow shoulders, its sleeves pulled halfway over her hands. She seemed content to let Akari supply the conversation.
“You asked me to choose the best photographs,” Sera said to Akari, “then took two more of the same chair.”
“The chair respects my process.”
“It hasn't moved,” Sera replied. “Your framing has.”
Akari turned to Andrew. “See? This is what I get for asking for help.”
“Sera's right,” Andrew said.
“I see,” Akari muttered. “Both of you are against me.”
Sera set one photograph on the smaller pile. “This one. The faces are in focus.”
Akari leaned over to inspect it. Their shoulders touched, and for a moment she forgot whatever complaint she'd intended to make.
Andrew reached for the coffee tin. It was empty.
“That's disappointing,” he said.
Akari swung the camera toward him. “Andrew! Chotto—wait, right there! That expression. Don't move.”
“Don't you dare.”
She took the photograph.
“Akari.”
“I'm calling it Man Discovers Empty Coffee Tin.”
“Gallery opening at noon?” Andrew asked.
“Only if you sit in the front row,” Akari said.

The common-room door opened before Andrew could invent an appropriate punishment. Mara Venn came in carrying a waterproof map case beneath one arm. As his appointed deputy, she handled patrol planning with a precision Andrew had learned to trust. At five foot eight she had a compact, athletic build, strong shoulders, and upright posture. Her long, dark chestnut hair was tied into a practical ponytail, with damp strands escaping around an angular face, high cheekbones, and a straight nose. Gray-green eyes swept over the room before settling on Andrew; the familiar line between her brows suggested she'd already found something that needed fixing. Her uniform was neat above the waist, though rain had darkened the fabric and mud marked her trouser cuffs and worn boots. She put a small packet beside the empty coffee tin.
“North watch,” she said. “They owed me a favor.”

Andrew inspected the packet. Real coffee, sealed and dry. Nobody had seen it in a regular supply allocation for months. He turned it over as if it might turn out to be a trick. “You are my favorite person.”
“You said that to Darius yesterday,” Mara reminded him.
“Darius made bread yesterday.”
Mara pulled out a chair. “Read the route changes before declaring favorites.”
Andrew filled the kettle and set it on the heater. “What changes?”
“Ja. The eastern crossing's flooding,” Mara said. Her German accent gave the short words a crisp edge. “We need another approach tomorrow.”

The relay station beyond the eastern works handled radio traffic between observation posts and the escorts bringing civilians and supplies toward the defended towns. It had been cutting out for days. A convoy had spent last night at a roadblock rather than enter the blind stretch, and the next supply run was due tomorrow evening. Andrew's unit had orders to secure a route for the technicians tomorrow morning and keep the road covered while they repaired the link.
Andrew had planned the most direct approach. Mara had spent the morning discovering why it might be a mistake.
“Let me get coffee,” he said, “and we'll spread the map out.”
“Gut,” Mara said. “I'll wait until the caffeine starts working.”
“That's very thoughtful.”
Akari raised her camera. “Everyone! Four o'clock, outside. All eight of us. New group photo.”
Mara didn't turn around. “Why?”
“The last group shot is ancient. I want a new one on the kitchen wall, and I want everybody in it.”
“It's raining,” Andrew said.
“Then the puddles will help with the light,” Akari said.
“Akari,” Sera said, “you're not taking your camera into the rain.”
“I know. If the rain stops,” Akari said.
“You didn't.”
“Ah, that's what I meant,” Akari said.
Sera handed Akari the photograph she'd selected. Akari smiled at it, slipped it into a protective sleeve, and looked back at the others.
“Four o'clock,” she repeated. “No disappearing into the hangar. I mean it.”
“Do I get a vote?” Andrew asked.
“Where you stand,” Akari answered. “I'll allow that.”
Mara unrolled the map. Andrew sat opposite her as the kettle began to hiss, grateful to have something useful to argue about.
From the kitchen came Darius's singing again. This time, Nico joined in from the corridor, deliberately half a beat behind.
By seven, Darius had filled the common room with the smell of toasted bread and apples.

He set the porridge in the middle of the table so that everyone could help themselves. There was enough for eight, provided Nico didn't start treating the serving spoon like a personal challenge. Darius stood beside the pot until Mara had taken a bowl and Yelena had arrived from the morning watch.
Andrew held up his own bowl. “You were right about the cinnamon.”
Darius raised an eyebrow. “More?”
“Just enough.”
“Thank you.” Darius tried to sound dignified, then smiled.
Nico took his first mouthful and stopped talking.
For a moment the only sounds were the spoon against his bowl and rain at the window.
“That good?” Darius asked.
Nico swallowed. “Attends—this is actually incredible.”
“It's porridge,” Mara said.
“Yes, I noticed. But with apples like these?” Nico went back for another mouthful.
“The last of them,” Darius said. “Enjoy it.”

Sera, sitting beside Akari, slid the remaining apple pieces toward Nico without looking up from a small puzzle book. Nico accepted them with a quiet thanks. Andrew noticed the gesture; Sera often gave things away when nobody was paying attention.

After breakfast Mara spread the map across the cleared table. The others drifted toward their assignments, leaving Andrew and Mara with two mugs of coffee and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub.
Mara touched the eastern crossing. “It's flooded. Yesterday the road markers were visible. This morning I could barely see their tops.”
“Can an XR-17 get through?” Andrew asked.
“Maybe. If the shoulder holds. One breakdown and there's no room to turn with a tow cable.”

Andrew pictured the crossing: a narrow bridge, soft ground beside the road, and fields that lay open on either side. The direct route had one advantage. It kept the squad close to the observation posts for most of the trip, which meant fewer places for the Reclaimed to approach unseen.
He could have argued for it. Part of him wanted to. He'd drawn that route himself.
Mara laid a second pencil line across the south edge of the map.
“Two kilometers longer,” Mara said. “Hard ground beyond the culvert. Paved recovery area at the old workshops. We can tow a damaged mech out without blocking the others.”
“What happens to our sightline at the culvert?”
“Three hundred meters of poor visibility,” Mara said. “Two mechs cover the approaches while the technicians pass.”
Andrew studied the small square she'd marked at the far end of the road.
“That's also where the convoy escorts check in,” he said.
Mara nodded. “If the relay goes down again, the next convoy waits too. They've got medical supplies for the clinic.”

The direct route was shorter. He still didn't like the extra blind stretch. But Mara had a clear recovery plan, and she'd gone out in the rain to check the surface instead of trusting the markings on the map.
“We'll use the service road,” Andrew said. “Mark the hardstand as our recovery point. Check with Yelena about west-watch coverage for the culvert.”
Mara looked at him. “No argument? Ach, I was prepared for one.”
“Would it unflood the bridge?”
“Probably not.”
“Then save us both the effort.”
She took the pencil. “You're learning.”
“I'll try not to make it a habit.”

Mara went back to the map. Andrew watched her mark the revised route, then added his initials beside the change. There was a time when he'd have taken a different plan as a challenge to his judgment. He remembered that version of himself with no particular affection.
“Thanks for checking it,” he said.
Mara's pencil stopped. “That's the job.”
“Still. Thanks.”
She gave him a quick nod and continued drawing.
At nine, the hangar doors opened just wide enough to admit the gray morning light.

Their eight XR-17s occupied a double row of maintenance bays. Each mech crouched on six articulated legs, its compact armored body hanging low between them. Scuffed plates concealed most of the internal structure, leaving the dark joints, pistons, and bundled cables exposed where the limbs needed to move. A heavy cannon sat above the cockpit on a rotating turret, flanked by matching vertical missile pods. Below the armored canopy, a smaller rotary cannon projected from the mech's nose. A circular reactor housing bulged from the rear.
The mechs had been manufactured to defend Germany when the rest of the world could no longer keep a defensive line intact. Their technology was impressive. Their maintenance records were less so.

One of Andrew's mechs had a mismatched foot. Another carried a panel salvaged from a destroyed vehicle. Replacement components still appeared on requisition forms, but increasingly the only way to get one was to strip it from something beyond repair. Every cockpit had its own collection of improvised fixes, nicknames, and tiny personal decorations that weren't in the manuals.
Juno Kade, the unit's lead mechanic as well as an XR-17 pilot, was under the left-front leg of his mech.

A few uneven tufts of vivid golden-blond hair stuck out beneath the orange-lensed goggles pushed up on Juno's head. Black headphones with orange detailing rested against the raised yellow collar of his dark mechanic's jacket, whose pockets were stained with grease and crowded with tools. A narrow strip of cyan trim ran along one shoulder. From where Andrew stood, only Juno's boots, one elbow, and part of his lean frame were visible beyond the mech's front armor.
“Morning,” Andrew called.
A metal tool clinked against the floor.
“Depends, mate,” Juno answered, the easy Australian vowels carrying from beneath the mech. “Something broke, or are ya here to ask when it'll be fixed?”
“Is the bearing coming out?”
“Yes.”
“Are you coming out?”
“When I've won this argument with the collar.”
Nico, the unit's radio technician when he wasn't piloting his own XR-17, knelt beside a tray of parts and lifted his hand. “I could pull him out.”
“Don't you dare, Nico,” Juno said.
A harsh scrape cut across the hangar. The tool Juno had been forcing against the stubborn collar slipped, striking the stand with a crack. Nico lurched backward, nearly upsetting the parts tray.
“Juno!” Nico shouted. “I told you! I told you we needed the proper extractor, not zat thing!”
Andrew crossed the space between them. “Out from under there. Now.”

Juno slid clear on the trolley, still clutching the improvised lever. At roughly five foot seven, he was slight and wiry, with narrow shoulders and grease-smeared forearms that never seemed to stop moving. Bright blue eyes stood out against the smudge across his cheek; a slightly pointed nose and narrow chin gave his youthful face an almost permanently mischievous look. Usually that look came with a grin. Right now he was more annoyed than frightened. “I had the collar moving. The tool slipped, that's all.”
“The tool was moving,” Nico said. His smile had vanished. “Toward your face.”
Juno gave the bar a guilty glance. “The stand took the force. It would've been fine.”

“No,” Andrew said. He kept his voice level, which was harder than raising it. “That joint's under load, and you know it. Get the extractor. I'm not having you gamble your hands because you're in a hurry.”
Juno's jaw tightened. For a second Andrew thought he would argue. Then Juno set the bar on the bench. “All right. I'll get it.”
“And Nico checks the setup with you before you start again,” Andrew added.
“I can do that,” Nico said. He was still watching the place the tool had struck.

With the proper extractor seated squarely over the joint, Juno backed out the retaining collar and drew the damaged left-front pivot bearing from its housing. The inner race came free with a scarred patch. He set the old assembly on the bench, saving its serviceable outer ring for workshop salvage.

“See the scoring?” Juno held the worn bearing up for Andrew. “That's why she catches under load. I've got a new one on the shelf. I'll clean the seat, press the replacement in straight, grease the pivot and torque the collar down. No point putting a ruined bearing back.”
“When can we test the leg?” Andrew asked.
“By two, mate. New bearing goes in before lunch. After that I check its travel and run my list: walking turn, loaded turn and one full-power cannon shot to see how she takes recoil.”
“Your repair, your checklist,” Andrew said. “Stop if you find anything else wrong.”
Juno nodded. He took care of his mech with a devotion Andrew wished he'd extend to his own hands.

In the next bay, Sera Bell sat on a crate with a diagnostic screen balanced across her knees. She had been following the readings throughout the repair, far less interested in the noise around her than the small errors appearing on the display.
“Juno. There's another fault,” Sera said.
Juno turned. “What? You said the bearing was the fault.”
“I said it was one fault,” Sera replied.
She angled the screen toward Andrew. Red spikes interrupted the smooth load graph every few seconds.
“Loose vibration pickup,” Sera explained. “False spikes on the left-side channel. The temperature and load readings are normal; those spikes aren't.”
Andrew looked at the raised leg. “It hasn't detached, right?”
Sera regarded him.
“No,” Sera said. “That would've been the first thing I told you.”
Juno grinned at her. “You really know how to reassure people.”
“I try,” Sera said without looking away from the screen.
As she unplugged the diagnostic lead, a folded page from the puzzle book she'd brought to breakfast slipped out from behind her tablet. She retrieved it before Nico could see the solution.
“Wait. Is that your solution?” Nico asked. “I've been stuck on that one all morning!”
“It's the solution,” Sera said, sliding it into her pocket. “Work it out yourself.”

Andrew stayed while Juno cleaned the empty pivot housing and pressed the replacement bearing into place with the service tool. Juno packed it with grease, refitted the retaining collar and tightened the fasteners to their marked settings. He cycled the suspended leg slowly through its travel. This time it moved without catching. The scored old bearing lay beside the replacement's empty wrapper on the bench.
“New bearing's in,” Juno said, ticking his repair sheet. “I'll reseat that vibration pickup and finish the clearances before I take her out.”
“You're not staying to supervise?” Juno asked.
“No,” Andrew said. “I'll watch the test. You know the work, and I expect you to run it properly.”
For a brief instant, Juno's expression lost its usual grin.
Juno looked back at the repaired pivot and picked up his torque wrench. “Right. No more shortcuts. Checklist all the way.”
“You'll survive.”
Nico held out the clipboard. “Can I put ‘no more heroics’ in the inspection log? As an official statement?”
“If you spell everything else correctly,” Andrew said.
Andrew left the hangar with the replacement bearing installed and Sera's diagnostic screen glowing beside the raised leg. Outside, the rain had thinned to a fine mist.
The north watch post overlooked a broad strip of land that might once have been pleasant countryside.

There were fields, a half-collapsed warehouse, and a road that ran toward the interior settlements. Beyond them sat a line of earthworks and concrete defenses. Farther east, the outposts became fewer, and Andrew tried not to think too long about what happened beyond the line on bad days.

Yelena Sokolova leaned against the watch post's railing with a dented metal mug cupped between her hands. She was around five foot seven, slender but sturdily built, with long limbs and a relaxed posture Andrew knew not to mistake for inattention. Cold had reddened her fair cheeks and straight nose. Her strong cheekbones and defined jaw made the raised eyebrow she gave him particularly effective, while pale gray eyes regarded him with their usual tired, unimpressed look. Her long ash-brown hair was braided thickly and tucked inside her military jacket, though the wind had pulled loose strands across her face. A bandage packet stuck out of an overfull pocket. She was their combat medic, but the shortage of hands meant she still drew regular watch shifts.
“On time for once,” Yelena said as Andrew climbed the stairs. Her Russian accent put a faint roll into the r, but there was no mistaking her dry delivery.
“I'm exactly on time.”
“Then someone's moved the clock.”
Andrew took the binoculars from the case. “Any movement?”
“Two patrol vehicles, one flatbed heading west, and a cat.”
“A cat?”
“Four legs. Hostile attitude. Keep an eye on it,” Yelena said.
Yelena pointed toward a narrow gap behind the storehouse. A small gray cat sat beneath the overhang, watching the rain.
Andrew lowered the binoculars. “You put water down for it.”
“Did I?”
“There's a dish beside it.”
“Perhaps it brought its own.”
“You're on the morning watch. Who else has been up here?”
Yelena sipped her tea instead of answering.
Beside her lay a paperback with two people standing on the cover in clothes far too clean for anyone Andrew knew. He turned it around to read the title.
“Is this the terrible book you were complaining about yesterday?”
“It's worse today,” Yelena said.
“You're nearly finished.”
“I want to know how bad it gets.”
Andrew read the summary on the back. “The main character is a veterinarian.”
Yelena took it gently from him. “Yes.”
“Does she ever do any veterinary work, or is this entirely about choosing between two identical men?”
“One dog,” Yelena replied. “Two pages of competent medicine.”
“Is that why you bought it?”
Yelena looked over the railing at the cat. “I didn't buy it. Someone left it here. The dog is the only sensible character.”

Andrew waited, but she didn't explain. He knew Yelena could help set a splint and find a fever before most of them realized someone was ill. She claimed it was because the unit was full of idiots who hurt themselves, but she had a habit of lingering near anything injured.
“You could do that after the war,” Andrew said.
Yelena gave him a sideways look. “Writing reviews of terrible books? Maybe.”
“Work with animals.”
“One cat,” she replied. “It will refuse to pay.”
Andrew smiled and turned back to the road.

A flatbed truck was approaching the outpost from the east. The driver slowed to wave, and Andrew recognized a woman who regularly traded produce and spare cloth for whatever useful repairs the mechanics could manage. There had been a time when she would have sent them a bill. Now she wanted working batteries, patched tires, or somebody willing to fix a broken heater.
He waved back.

The vehicle continued toward the settlements. People were still moving materials, repairing roofs, and growing food in places that had been damaged a dozen times. The defensive line existed to give them room for those ordinary things.
Yelena nodded toward the road. “One convoy's already been held up by that relay. If it fails again tomorrow, the next one doesn't move either.”
“We're escorting the repair team tomorrow morning,” Andrew said. “Mara's found us a way around the flooded crossing.”
“Good.” Yelena picked up a folded note from the watch log. “New water readings. Took them after breakfast.”
She had written down the levels at the eastern drainage channel. The water was climbing faster than Mara's earlier report suggested.
Andrew radioed Mara with the new readings. She acknowledged the update and confirmed the service road was still their best approach.
“How much sleep did you get?” Yelena asked without looking at him.
“Enough.”
“How much is enough?”
Andrew considered giving her a joke. She had asked him the same question twice that week.
“Not quite,” he admitted.
“Get more tonight,” Yelena said.
“Are you giving medical advice?”
“Yes. Sleep before piloting a mech,” Yelena replied.
Andrew looked at the tea mug in her hand. “You could have said you were worried.”
“Da. You already know,” Yelena said.

He left her at the railing, checking her written water readings against the road. As he descended the stairs, the gray cat finally ventured out from beneath the overhang. Yelena pretended not to watch it cross toward the dish.
Darius's garden stood against the kitchen wall.

He'd built the beds from old transport crates and covered them with clear panels scavenged from storage. The plants were small and uneven but plainly alive. Andrew paused on his way to the hangar and found Darius kneeling beside a row of herbs.
“Checking on my plants?” Darius asked without looking up.
“Just checking whether we're going to have a salad sometime this decade.”
“They've only been out here three weeks, Andrew. Give them a chance.”
“Sorry. I didn't know they were sensitive.”
Darius touched a leaf. “The nights are still too cold. I'm hoping these covers help.”
“Same.”
Darius rose, brushing soil from his palms. There was a little pride in the way he surveyed the beds, as if they'd accomplished something extraordinary.
“What are you making tonight?” Andrew asked.
“Stew,” Darius said. “Potatoes, beans, onions, cabbage. Maybe some herbs, if these plants cooperate. Enough for everybody.”
“Can I help?”
“Keep Nico from eating dinner before it's ready.”
“That's a full-time assignment.”

Darius smiled, then grew more thoughtful. “Actually... would you make sure everybody's back before I start? Yelena's done two watches today. And Sera will lose track of the time if she gets into a puzzle.”
Andrew nodded. “I'll round them up.”
Darius reached for his watering can. “And please remind Juno that the kitchen isn't part of the workshop, s'il te plaît.”
“What did he take this time?”
“Nothing,” Darius replied. “I'd like to keep it that way.”
The XR-17 test began shortly after two. Juno had fitted the new bearing, greased the pivot and checked its movement in the hangar. Now he wanted to see how it held under the mech's full weight.

He walked his XR-17 into the yard with his checklist clipped beside the cockpit display. The six feet settled in a deliberate rhythm on the concrete. The cannon and missile pods stayed secured until the authorized live-fire test.

Andrew, Mara, Sera and Nico stood behind the yard's safety line. Mara held the telemetry tablet; Sera watched beside her and Nico leaned against the barrier. Juno had the controls, the tools and the checklist. The others were there to observe.
“First check: slow walk,” Juno said over the radio. “New left-front bearing seated, collar torqued, grease feed clear. Temperature normal. Moving to the turn markers.”
He guided the XR-17 through a slow right arc and then a left. The repaired foot lifted and settled smoothly where it had caught the previous day.
Mara checked the tablet. “Bearing temperature normal. Joint load steady. No abnormal vibration.”
“Acknowledged,” Juno said. “Loaded turn next.” He ticked the first test off himself.
He shifted the mech's weight and started the next maneuver. Halfway to the final marker, he stopped.
“Holding,” Juno said. “Vibration at the left rear. Not the bearing.”
The XR-17 stayed planted while he checked his cockpit indicators. “Feels like an exterior panel. I'm going back in to check it.”
Mara watched a second trace rise. “Confirmed. Left-front readings are clean. The vibration's farther back.”
Andrew kept his hands off the radio. Juno had identified the fault and stopped without anybody telling him to.
“Loaded-turn check paused,” Juno announced. “Returning to the apron. I'll repeat it once the bracket's secure.”

He brought his XR-17 back at a crawl, powered down and locked the legs. Juno opened the left-rear access panel, found a loose bracket and tightened its fastener. He checked the neighboring mounts before sealing it up again. Nobody stepped in to do his work for him.
On the second attempt the loaded turn was clean. Mara acknowledged the steady temperature and vibration readings; Juno checked the step off and headed for the range.

The live-fire lane lay beyond the rear earthworks, with an observation shelter behind a concrete wall. Rain had darkened the target posts and left the service track muddy. At the far end, a reinforced practice target waited in front of a high dirt backstop.
The range had authorized one full-power cannon discharge. Juno would use it to check the new bearing under recoil, not simply to put a hole in the target.
All of them knew how an XR-17 braced itself before a shot. Today the point was to see whether Juno's repair could take it.
Juno brought the XR-17 onto the firing mark and spread its six legs into a stable stance. Above the cockpit, the turret lined up with the target; the vertical missile pods remained secured.
Andrew stood inside the shelter with Sera and Nico. Mara positioned her tablet where she could follow the left-front load trace.
“Live-fire checklist,” Juno said. “Range authorization received. Target area clear. Missile pods safe. Turret aligned.”
Mara looked at the screen. “Temperature normal. Load settled.”
Nico leaned toward Andrew. “He's actually checking every box.”
“Course I am,” Juno replied. “Recoil braces next.”
Andrew smiled. He'd promised to watch, not hover over Juno's shoulder.
“Braces locked,” Juno said. “Main cannon ready. Waiting for the range-clear indicator.”
The light above the shelter window turned green. The same clearance appeared on Juno's cockpit display.
“Range clear,” Juno continued. “Bearing load within limits. Weapon safeties released for one discharge.”
He marked the final item on his checklist. “All checks complete. Charging the cannon.”
Nico leaned closer to the glass. Nobody interrupted the pilot.
“Readings acknowledged. Left-front trace steady,” Mara said.

Beyond the glass, the XR-17's rear reactor brightened. A low vibration rolled across the ground as the cannon charged. Heat stirred the air around the barrel, and thin lines of white-gold light came alive along its length.
Nico leaned forward. He'd fired the same weapon during training, but watching someone else's cannon charge never got old.
“Firing,” Juno announced. “Three... two... one.”
The cannon discharged.
A column of white-hot energy tore downrange. The shelter shook as the report hit, hard enough that Andrew felt it through the soles of his boots. Dust leapt from the firing lane.

The target vanished inside the impact. The beam carried through to the hillside beyond, carving a brilliant wound in the dirt backstop. For an instant the earth glowed orange-white, then slumped inward, glassy where the heat had fused the soil.
The XR-17 rocked backward. Its six legs dug in, absorbed the force and brought the hull level again. Andrew watched the repaired left-front pivot compress and recover without a hitch.
Mara kept her eyes on the load graph as its peak began to fall.
“Did you see that?” Juno shouted over the radio. “Not a single foot lifted!”
Nico laughed. “You're more excited about its feet than the crater.”
“That's the part he repaired,” Sera said, still watching the mech.
“Load traces returned to baseline,” Mara acknowledged.
Andrew grinned. Juno had handled the repair, caught a second fault and worked through every check himself.
“Post-fire inspection,” Juno said. “Weapon safe. Cooling normal. Left-front pivot...”
He paused to read his cockpit display. “No binding. That's a clean recovery.”
“Confirmed,” Mara said. “Joint load steady.”
“All that work for one bearing,” Nico murmured.
“One bearing that keeps my mech standing,” Juno answered.
Across the range, steam rose from the crater. The XR-17 stood level on its repaired leg, cannon cooling above the cockpit.
Mara checked the last graph. “Peak recoil within tolerance. No residual vibration.”
“Seriously?” Juno asked. “Even at peak?”
“Even at peak,” Mara replied.
“HA! THAT'S IT!” Juno shouted.
His delight crackled through the radio loudly enough to make Nico pull off one ear cup.
“You care more about the bearing than the crater,” Andrew said.
“I replaced the bearing,” Juno replied. “The cannon was always going to make a crater.”
“Final checklist item: return to hangar, walking speed,” Juno said. “Weapon secured.”
“Any chance I could have another crack at it?” he added.
Mara glanced at the authorization entry. “One approved discharge. One used.”
“Worth asking,” Juno said.
He turned the XR-17 toward the depot. Nico imitated the cannon's roar while Mara continued to watch the cooling trace.
Back in the hangar, Juno powered the mech down, climbed out and examined the repaired leg. The others watched as he checked the retaining collar, pivot seal and alignment marks.
“No movement,” Juno said, ticking the final box. “New bearing's holding.”
Mara checked the display. “Temperature and recoil readings normal. No lingering vibration.”
Juno signed his repair sheet. “Test complete. XR-17 cleared for duty.”
“Good work,” Andrew said. Juno glanced at the replaced bearing's housing, his usual grin settling into something smaller and genuinely pleased.
Outside, the rain had started again. Juno glanced toward the yard and the empty camera tripod. “Mate, I was hoping Akari could get a photo while the mech was clean.”
“Akari's working on it,” Andrew said.
As if she'd heard her name, Akari appeared in the doorway. “Hai! Four o'clock, everyone. No disappearing.”
Mara looked past her at the wet concrete. “It's raining.”
“I have a plan,” Akari said.
Andrew looked at her determined face. He doubted the weather would get the last word.
At four seventeen, Akari declared the weather officially cooperative.

The rain had stopped, although water still dripped from the gutters. She set the tripod on a dry patch of concrete and inspected the viewfinder with an expression usually reserved for people checking a weapon sight.
Mara came out of the hangar first, carrying her folded route sheet.
“How long?” Mara asked Akari.
“Depends. Can you all cooperate for ten seconds?” Akari replied.
“Unlikely,” Mara said.
Akari ignored her and adjusted the camera again.

Andrew had spent the last ten minutes collecting the squad. Yelena had wanted to finish her watch log, Darius had checked the bread dough, and Nico had vanished to find a respectable jacket. He'd returned wearing one with a torn elbow.
Sera was already by the tripod, helping Akari keep the lens clean.
“Your spare battery,” Sera told her.
“I had that on my list. Somewhere,” Akari replied.
“You said that about the lens cloth and the tripod,” Sera said.
“Because you keep saving the day. Again,” Akari said.
Sera placed the battery into Akari's hand. “Remember it next time.”
“I'll owe you a favor,” Akari said.
“You already do,” Sera replied.
Sera straightened the tripod while Akari checked her framing. They had a way of making the same argument sound like teamwork.
Juno emerged with his goggles in his bright hair, still looking pleased with his repair.
“Juno? Something on your mind? Say it,” Akari said.
“Reckon the picture'd look better if we angled the turret toward us?” Juno asked. “No firing, obviously.”
Mara folded her arms. “Not today.”
“I know,” Juno said. He didn't argue.
Andrew had heard quite enough about that cannon for one afternoon.
Akari waved him toward the group. “Then come over here. You're taller than the tripod. Use that talent.”
Juno looked at the battered XR-17. “Can I at least stand on the good side?”
“Which side would that be?” Sera asked.
Juno gave her a pained look, then grinned despite himself.

The eight of them gathered beneath the broad front of the center XR-17. Its six legs framed the group, the angular cockpit hanging above them. Against the enormous feet and heavy armored body, even Darius looked smaller than usual.
“Closer, Nico! No, a little to the left—there! Now closer to Darius,” Akari called from the tripod.
Nico shuffled sideways and bumped Darius's shoulder.
“Two steps, Nico. That's not enough,” Akari repeated.
Nico pressed against Darius so firmly that Darius nearly lost his balance.
“Mou! Not that close! Leave the poor man room to breathe,” Akari said.
“You said closer!” Nico protested. “I'm trying. There are only so many places for my feet.”
Yelena took Nico by the back of his jacket and pulled him into a less dangerous position.
“Here,” Yelena told him. “Davai. Stay.”
“I can't help it. It's stuck in my head,” Nico explained.
“Try humming internally,” Yelena told him.
Mara moved beside Andrew. Her uniform trousers were still marked by the mud from the morning inspection.
“If this picture ends up on the official noticeboard,” Mara said, “I want my objection recorded.”
“Your objection is noted,” Andrew replied. “On an unofficial basis.”
Akari waved from the camera. “Andrew! Mara! Eyes here, please.”
“We're looking,” Mara said.
“Good. Now hold still,” Akari called.
Sera crouched, checked the camera's focus one last time, then stood and joined the others. Akari set the timer for ten seconds and ran toward the group.
At six seconds, she saw the camera strap dangling across the corner of the lens.
“Ah! Wait, don't move!” Akari called.
She doubled back, fixed the strap, and tried again. At three seconds Nico stepped onto Mara's boot. Mara reached for his arm, but Nico tipped toward Juno, who caught him by the collar.
Andrew started laughing.
Akari made it into place just as the camera clicked.
For a moment she stood there breathing hard, then hurried back to the tripod.
“Did you get everyone?” Darius asked.
Akari inspected the screen. “Oh.”

The others gathered around her, passing the camera carefully from hand to hand. The picture was a disaster by any official standard. Nico's eyes were wide with alarm, Mara was holding Juno's sleeve, and Andrew had his head turned toward the commotion. Akari was still moving into position, her ponytail caught halfway through a swing.
Darius had somehow managed to smile normally.
“That's the one,” Darius said. “I want it above the table.”
Mara stared at the image. “No.”
Akari held the camera to her chest. “Yes. Look at it. It's perfect.”
“Can we at least take one where I'm standing properly?” Mara asked.
“Of course,” Akari said. “But I like this one.”
Sera glanced at the screen again. “Me too.”
Andrew studied the photograph. No one looked disciplined or heroic. They looked like themselves on an ordinary afternoon, still arguing over where to stand.
“Print that one, Akari,” Andrew said.
Darius was already studying the space above the kitchen table.
By the time the courtyard emptied, Akari had shown everyone the photograph at least twice. She promised to print it as soon as she could find paper that would survive their ancient printer.

Juno stayed in the hangar long enough to put his tools away. The worn bearing sat in a salvage tray, its damaged inner race separated from the good metal he hoped to reuse. Nico had offered to help sort it; Juno had told him that sorting meant putting things into piles, not inventing new names for them.
Andrew left the two of them arguing cheerfully over a label and went to finish the paperwork for tomorrow's escort.
When he emerged, the common room was filling up. Darius had kept his promise of stew, and the others had arrived in time to eat it.

Nobody made a ceremony of dinner. They passed bowls and bread around the table, talked over one another, and complained about the tiny print on tomorrow's duty schedule. Darius took his own seat instead of standing by the stove to ask whether everyone liked what he'd made.
“You're eating with us,” Andrew observed.
“I do that sometimes,” Darius said.
“Usually after making three trips to see if anyone wants more.”
“Then don't let me get up.”
Andrew nudged the bread toward him. Darius accepted a piece and stayed where he was.
At the far end of the table, Juno was describing the cannon test for the third time, complete with a broad sweep of both hands.
“And the leg took the recoil beautifully, mate. Not a bit of binding.”
“We know,” Sera said. “We watched.”
“Watching and appreciating are different things.”
“I acknowledged the readings,” Mara said, deadpan. “Does that count?”
“I'll put you down as impressed.”
“Don't falsify my statement.”
Akari tried to catch Mara's expression with her camera. Mara turned away a second too late.
“Another one for the wall!” Akari declared.
“There isn't that much wall,” Mara said.
“We'll find more.”

By the time the bowls were empty, someone had pushed the table aside to make room for movie night. Yelena produced her worn deck of cards, and Darius leaned back in his chair with the wary expression of someone who'd been invited into a trap.
“Rematch,” Yelena said. “Davai.”
“You still owe me two biscuits.”
“I won those.”
“You ate them before the game.”
“And won afterward. Different events.”
Darius appealed to Andrew, who held up his hands. “I'm not getting involved.”
“Coward,” Darius said, smiling.
Yelena dealt the cards. Mara joined the next hand and discovered within minutes that Yelena's explanation of the rules seemed to change depending on who was winning.
“This is not the game you taught me,” Mara said.
“You're learning,” Yelena replied.
Near the projector, Nico had begun tapping a rhythm on the edge of a wooden chair. He stopped whenever somebody looked at him, then started again a little more quietly.
Sera was trying to align the screen. “You keep losing the fourth beat,” she said.
“I'm not losing it. I'm leaving space.”
“Then the space has an irregular duration.”
Juno looked up from the headphones around his neck. “Sounds all right to me.”
“It's not finished,” Nico said quickly.
“What's not finished?” Akari asked, already turning toward him.
“Nothing. Just something I'm messing around with.”
She dropped into a chair opposite him. “Well, do it again. I missed the beginning.”
Nico looked at Andrew as though requesting rescue. Andrew only shrugged.
“You don't have to play it for us,” Andrew said. “But I'd listen.”
“It's barely a song.” Nico drummed the opening again, softer this time. Then he hummed three rising notes, hesitated, and tried a different ending.

The room wasn't suddenly silent. Yelena dealt another hand. Someone shifted a chair. But Nico kept going, and for a few seconds Andrew could hear what he'd been trying to build out of all those half-finished rhythms.
When Nico stopped, he studied his hands.
“It's a start,” Sera said. “I liked the second ending.”
“Me too,” Darius said from the card table.
“You weren't even listening,” Nico protested.
“I can lose at cards and listen to music at the same time, mon ami.”
“He's very practiced at losing,” Yelena added.
Darius laid down a card. “You have no idea how the rest of this hand is going to go.”
Nico ducked his head, but Andrew caught his grin. A moment later he began tapping the melody again, less afraid of being heard.
Sera found the projector remote under a cushion. “Movie. My choice tonight.”
“You picked last time,” Akari objected.
“Last time you made us watch the bird documentary.”
“Which was wonderful!”
“I was awake for the eagle,” Nico offered.
“That's not an endorsement,” Sera said.
“What are we watching?” Andrew asked.
“A comedy. Nobody tells me the ending.”
Nico opened his mouth.
“Guessing the ending out loud counts,” Sera added.
“I wasn't going to!”
Akari made a disbelieving noise. Mara finally laughed, and Nico looked pleased with himself even as he protested.
Sera switched on the projector while Yelena collected another set of cards from the table.
The projector came on, its picture leaning slightly to the left. Sera watched it for a second, folded a square of cardboard, and pushed it beneath the rear foot. The image straightened on the wall.
Juno looked over from his headphones. “That mount needs a new bracket. The cardboard'll slip once the room warms up.”
“The film's ninety minutes,” Sera said. “The cardboard will last that long.”
Juno considered the argument, then went back to his seat.

Andrew leaned against the arm of the couch while they settled in. Mara occupied a chair with her boots tucked beneath it. Nico took the seat closest to the projector, insisting that it had the best sound, though he'd spent most of the afternoon complaining about the film choice.
Sera started her comedy without inviting another vote.
For the opening ten minutes, Nico tried to explain how he would handle every situation differently. Sera gave him a look. Nico held up his hands and, with impressive effort, stopped talking.

Andrew laughed at a scene in which a man tried to smuggle food out of a banquet under his coat. It was the sort of ridiculous problem the actors treated with such seriousness that he couldn't help enjoying it.
He stayed through the next scene, too.
Then he checked the wall clock.
One handover note remained for tomorrow's technicians. Five minutes, Andrew told himself.
He slipped off the arm of the couch.
Akari noticed. “Andrew? Where are you going?”
“Office,” Andrew said. “Five minutes.”
“That's what you said last night,” Akari replied.
“I did come back.”
“After the credits.”
Andrew couldn't deny it. He promised to be quicker this time and slipped into the corridor.
The corridor was cooler than the common room. He passed the kitchen, where the pans were drying on a rack, and reached his small office beside the hangar.
The small office held a desk, two chairs and a filing cabinet. His lamp lit a map of tomorrow's route; a spare pair of gloves still hung from a nail beside the door.

Mara's revised route was clear on the map. The flooded bridge was marked off, the alternate road checked, and the escort's waiting point agreed. He had already seen the signatures. An old duty roster was caught beneath the edge of the map, its twelve name slots still filled in. Andrew slid it out of the way without reading them, then opened his notebook anyway.
Andrew wrote the handover note and set his pen down. There was nothing else that needed his attention tonight.
An old photograph was pinned beside the desk lamp.

Twelve people stood crowded between two XR-17s, several of them laughing before the camera had even been set. The picture had been taken when the whole original unit was together. Their uniforms looked newer, and Matthias Adler stood at the back with two fingers hooked into Andrew's collar.
Andrew remembered Matthias doing it just as Akari called for everybody to stand still. He'd been laughing and trying to pull away when the camera clicked.

Matthias had been twenty-one, and somehow capable of making every terrible joke sound like an official order. He'd claimed the photograph proved that Andrew was too impatient to stand still for ten seconds.
Andrew touched the edge of the paper.

Four people in the old picture no longer came to breakfast. Sometimes an everyday thing reminded him of one of them: an argument over a game, an empty place by the repair bench, a song somebody used to complain about and now played without thinking.
He knew the four missing faces well enough. He didn't need to make the photograph teach him anything.

Earlier that afternoon Akari had taken another picture, this time of the eight who were still together. He remembered Mara holding Juno's sleeve, Nico nearly falling, and Akari barely making it into the frame.
He found himself smiling.
A knock interrupted him.
Darius stood in the doorway holding a little plate and a jar.
“Still working?” Darius asked.
“Just finished.” Andrew closed his notebook.
“Good. Then I've brought dessert,” Darius said.
He set a small plate and a jar on Andrew's desk. The roll was split and toasted; Darius spread strawberry jam across it with the care he gave anything he made for a friend.
Andrew read the label.
“Strawberry?” he asked. “Where did you get that?”
“I know people,” Darius said.
“What sort of people?” Andrew asked.
“People who appreciate bread.”
Andrew took a bite. The toast was crisp and warm, and the sweetness tasted better than anything from a ration tin.
“That's really good,” he said.
“It's jam and bread.”
“Don't undersell yourself.”
Darius lingered beside the cabinet, glancing at the old photograph by the lamp.
“Did Akari say when she can print the new picture?” Darius asked.
“As soon as the printer cooperates. She's already threatened it twice.”
“Good. I've cleared a space above the table.”
“Even after seeing Nico step on Mara's boot?”
“Especially after seeing that.”
Andrew smiled into his toast. “Mara might object.”
“She already has. I'm sure she'll object to the frame too.”
“You'll let her choose it, won't you?”
“Absolutely not,” Darius said with an easy smile.
Andrew took another bite before Darius could reach across and straighten the uneven edge of his notebook.

From the common room came a burst of laughter, then a familiar voice protesting that the film's main character was making a terrible decision. Nico's voice. It had a distinctive way of climbing whenever he felt that an imaginary person ought to listen to his advice.
Darius glanced toward the door. “They're waiting for you.”
Andrew glanced from the photograph to the finished note. “You're right.”
He rose from his chair.
“Come on,” he said. “Before Nico starts directing the film himself.”
Darius stepped aside and let him pass.

The common room had grown warm and crowded. Akari had claimed the couch beside Sera, who was watching the film with the pleased concentration of someone whose choice had finally been accepted. Yelena and Mara were following the story from the chairs, occasionally exchanging a comment. Nico sat on the floor with a cushion behind his back, still whispering occasional advice to the actors.
Juno looked up as Andrew came back.
“Everything sorted?” Juno asked.
“Enough for tonight,” Andrew said.
“Good. We saved you a spot.” Juno nodded toward the couch.
“Appreciate it,” Andrew said.
“No worries, mate,” Juno replied.
Andrew squeezed onto the couch beside Akari. She lifted her feet for him to sit, then draped them across his knees. “I charge for this,” he told her.
“Put it on my account,” Akari said without looking away from the screen.

Darius returned to his card game with Yelena, who had somehow persuaded Mara into a rematch. Andrew balanced his plate on one hand, trying to decide whether the film's leading man was supposed to be clever or simply lucky.
Akari reached for his toast.
He caught her wrist gently.
“Ask Darius,” Andrew whispered.
“I did,” she whispered back. “He said you'd share.”
Across the room Darius looked up, met Andrew's eyes, and gave him an unapologetic shrug.
Andrew broke the toast in half.
Akari accepted her share with a satisfied smile. On the wall the hero finally escaped through the window, only to discover that he'd climbed into the wrong garden.
Nico groaned. Sera laughed. Even Mara covered her mouth.
Andrew stayed until the credits.
